name: Prostatilen

lead: Prostatilen is a peptide extract from cattle prostate, developed in the Soviet Union and used in Russia and nearby countries for prostatitis and prostate enlargement. Longevity circles list it with other Khavinson bioregulators as a general-health option. It is a urology product, not a cosmetic one.

The chain runs from a tissue-specific prostate extract to urological support to general health. Early-1990s Russian reports looked at prostatitis, rat studies report changes in prostate size and oxidative-stress markers, and a 2026 paper examined prostate-derived peptide preparations and erectile function in men with chronic prostatitis.

paras: Clinically it is given in courses for prostate conditions in post-Soviet countries. In longevity circles it appears alongside other bioregulator peptides.
Safety information comes mostly from regional studies; two older mouse studies examined mutagenicity. It is not a Western-approved drug, and independent trials are not documented.

angle.text: Prostatilen is a bovine prostate extract used in post-Soviet urology for prostatitis and enlargement, and mentioned in bioregulator discussions as a general-health option. Data is mostly Russian-language clinical work; no appearance use is described.

lead: Prostatilen is a peptide preparation extracted from the prostate glands of cattle. It was developed in the Soviet Union in the mid-1980s and has been used in Russia, Ukraine and other post-Soviet countries for chronic prostatitis and benign prostatic hyperplasia, according to Grokipedia [1]. It belongs to the family of organ-derived peptide bioregulators, or cytomedins, associated with Vladimir Khavinson's research group [2][3].

Prostatilen is a urology product rather than a cosmetic one. Its link to looks is indirect and claimed: people who use prostate-health and longevity peptides describe goals such as urinary comfort, sexual function and general vitality, which they associate with feeling and appearing younger [2]. No study has measured appearance outcomes.

Published human studies are largely Russian-language reports on prostatitis, prostatic adenoma and male infertility, plus experimental work in rats and mice [4][5][6][7][8][9][4]. A 2026 paper examined prostate-derived complex peptide preparations and erectile function in men with chronic prostatitis [10]. Trials by independent Western groups have not been published.
infobox: Chronic prostatitis, benign prostatic hyperplasia (post-Soviet states) [1]

paras: According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, Prostatilen consists of low-molecular-weight peptides obtained by ultrafiltration of a bovine prostate extract, and is supplied as suppositories and as a powder for intramuscular injection [1]. Variants combining the extract with zinc or arginine are also described there [1].

Vladimir Khavinson (1946-2024) was a Russian gerontologist who led the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and promoted peptide bioregulators, small protein fragments, as geroprotectors intended to slow ageing [3]. Wikipedia credits him with extracting more than 20 peptide complexes from organs between 1973 and 2013 and synthesising 15 more, and lists Prostatilen among six peptide preparations approved for medical use in the USSR, Russia and later CIS countries, with the others being Thymalin, Epithalamin, Cortexin, Retinalamin and Thymogen [3].

Wikipedia describes Prostatilen, also sold as Samprost or Vitaprost, as a preparation derived from the prostate gland that acts as a regulator of prostate function [3]. Khavinson's group summarised the clinical efficacy of its bioregulators, Prostatilen included, in a 2013 review in Advances in Gerontology [2]. Most claims for these peptides, including their safety, originate from Khavinson's own group and, per Wikipedia's article, are not independently verified there; the article carries a notice about promotional content [3].

Early Russian-language papers from 1991 report its use in patients with prostatic diseases and chronic prostatitis, including prostatitis accompanied by sexual dysfunction [11][7][8]. Grokipedia states that early trials reported symptom improvement in most patients, a claim it does not tie to controlled data [1]. A review by Khavinson's group lists Prostatilen among bioregulators with clinical efficacy in prevention and treatment [2].

A 2006 clinical study in Urologiia examined repeated courses of Prostatilen suppositories combined with dimexide in men with prostatic adenoma and normal micturition, and reported reduced symptoms of infravesical obstruction and residual urine volume [12]. A 2003 comparative report described urological experience with the drug [13]. A 2017 review of Russian studies of Vitaprost Forte suppositories, a related prostate-extract product, reported reduced dysuria and improved quality of life in men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia [14]. In a 2022 phase III open-label trial of 98 men with chronic abacterial prostatitis and impaired sperm parameters, a version of Prostatilen with added zinc arginyl-glycinate was compared with plain Prostatilen over 10 days [15]. A 2026 open-label randomised study of 60 men compared Prostatex Plus with Prostatilen over 20 days using NIH-CPSI, IPSS and IIEF-5 questionnaires [16]. A 2026 report examined prostate-derived peptide preparations and erectile function in chronic prostatitis [10].
Reports are mostly from the developers' regional literature and open-label designs, and independent replication is not documented.

In rats with experimentally induced prostatic hyperplasia, Prostatilen was reported to prevent increases in prostate size and to alter oxidative-stress markers, with an effect comparable to a saw palmetto extract in one study [9][2]. A 1995 report in male rats described stimulating effects on spermatogenesis and testicular androgen function [4]. Two 1990s mouse studies examined its mutagenicity and how vitamin C or immobilisation modified it [5][6].

Prostatilen appears in longevity-peptide discussions alongside other Khavinson preparations [2]. On T Nation, prostate health, testing and supplements are discussed in threads on finasteride and prostate screening, where posters debate supplements and screening rather than Prostatilen specifically [17][18]. It is marketed as a medicine in Russia and Ukraine and is not a Western-approved drug [1].
